items.title: Tommy Ridgley Interview, 1986-03-22
items.q: Now, most of your better musicians in the city today, like Red Tyler, Earl Palmer, Ernest McLean, all of the people who really wound up being musicians in the top, they came from Greenwald.

ctx.x: I would sing, you know. But, um, and musically, I would think of that. First of all, first of all, first of all, first I started to go to, uh, I would sing, you know.

And, uh, I would sing, you know. But, um, and musically, I would think of what I wanted to do. Um, I had this singing thing was always in the back of my mind. I would sing, you know. But, um, and musically, I would think, first of all, first I started to go to, first I started to go back in the service, okay, I threw that out. That stayed in my mind a long time. Then I decided, I'm going to go to Barber College. I won't be no Barber. So, and then when I started singing, I said, well, I'm going to go to music…
That's that. So once you got into Greenwald, what was your day like? What was your instruction like?

items.title: Tommy Ridgley Interview, 1986-04-23
items.q: T-Gym was a tune that Tyler had wrote

ctx.x: Yeah. And your big song with Dekka was Tra La La.

Okay, yeah, well that's something to talk about. Was Tra La La story? Okay, I wrote Tra La La. I never forget how I wrote it. I wrote Tra La La. See, because it was that Lord of Miss Claude kind of progression again. Laying across my bed, I'm living on Andover Street. That's how I wrote the song. And I had a little piano out on a porch that used to cut down bang on. Well then I wrote that song there and I had this song and I told it to everybody. So we finally got around to recording. Never did have a flip side…
Now my record came out doing fantastic.
